4.2 Feedback on the public consultation AMLA publicly consulted on the draft proposal contained in this paper. The consultation period lasted for three months and ended on 9th May 2026. 211 answers were received, of which 204 were valid8. Respondents were geographically represented across more than 25 Member States, and also across other countries outside of the EU. 45% of the respondents represented industry associations, 30% of the respondents were obliged entities, the rest were civil society organisations, self-regulated bodies or service providers. Regarding the sectors, a good balance was reached between financial and non-financial sector respondents.

This section presents a summary of the key points arising from the consultation, the analysis and discussion triggered by these comments and the actions taken to address them if deemed necessary. Changes to the draft proposal have been incorporated as a result of the responses received during the public consultation.

4.2.1 SUMMARY OF KEY ISSUES AND AMLA’S RESPONSE Respondents expressed support for the draft RTS, and for reinforcing the risk-based approach underpinning the AMLR. Feedback mainly focused on requests for clarification and further detail, rather than requests for changes to the overall structure or policy choices. In response, AMLA introduced clarifications to improve clarity and readability. The sections below describe, where relevant, how the draft RTS were amended to reflect the comments received.

1) Legal certainty concerning business relationships, occasional transactions and linked transactions A recurring theme throughout the consultation concerned the need for greater legal certainty regarding the key concepts used in the RTS.

Respondents commented extensively on Article 1 and questioned the practical usefulness of defining "occasional transaction" solely by reference to the absence of a business relationship. Several respondents considered that the negative definition provides limited operational guidance and may be difficult to apply where obliged entities provide services connected to transactions rather than carrying out transactions themselves. Respondents also expressed concerns that, under a negative definition, every interaction between an obliged entity and a person would need to be classified either as a business relationship or as an occasional transaction.
8 209 valid responses were received, of which 204 were taken into account after removing multiple submissions,

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 19( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 27 In addition, respondents commented on Recital 4 and the interaction between the Level 1 definitions and the criteria contained in Articles 2 and 3 of the RTS. Several stakeholders questioned the recital's statement that business relationships and linked transactions may exist even where none of the RTS criteria are present. They argued that this could create legal uncertainty and increase the risk of divergent supervisory interpretations across Member States.
AMLA’s response AMLA carefully considered the comments relating to legal certainty and the interaction between the AMLR definitions and the criteria set out in the RTS.

The concepts of business relationships and linked transactions are already defined in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 and should remain the primary reference for obliged entities when assessing whether those concepts are met. The purpose of the RTS is not to redefine these concepts, but to specify criteria that should be taken into account when assessing certain elements of the definitions already provided by Level 1. The criteria set out in Articles 2 and 3 are therefore not exhaustive and should not be interpreted as limiting the scope of the Level 1 definitions. Accordingly, the absence of one or more of the RTS criteria does not, in itself, preclude the existence of a business relationship or linked transactions where, based on the relevant facts and circumstances, the conditions set out in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 are otherwise met. Recital 4 is intended to clarify this relationship between the Level 1 definitions and the RTS criteria and to ensure that the latter are not treated as a closed list.

AMLA further considers that defining occasional transactions by reference to the absence of a business relationship remains the most consistent approach, as it avoids regulatory gaps and overlaps between the two concepts. In light of the comments received, AMLA amended Recital 5 to clarify that the Regulation applies only to activities falling within the scope of the AML/CFT framework. Therefore, transactions conducted where the obliged entity is itself the customer, for instance in its dealings with utility providers, are neither business relationships nor occasional transactions for the purposes of this Regulation.

2) Distinguishing online registration from the establishment of a business relationship Comments relating to Article 2(1) and Recital 7 were among the most frequently recurring throughout the consultation. More than sixty respondents, particularly from the crypto-asset, payment services, fintech, gambling, credit intermediation, real estate and professional services sectors, questioned the use of online registration as an indicator of duration. Respondents argued that registration is often merely a technical prerequisite for accessing a service and does not necessarily indicate an intention to establish an ongoing relationship. Several stakeholders

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 19( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 28 highlighted that customers may register on platforms, compare products, access information, receive alerts or maintain dormant accounts without ever engaging in transactions or services falling within the scope of the AML/CFT framework.

Consequently, many respondents considered that the current drafting risks classifying irrelevant interactions as business relationships and may lead to disproportionate customer due diligence obligations.
AMLA’s response:
AMLA acknowledges the concerns expressed regarding the treatment of registration as an indicator of duration.

To address these concerns, AMLA amended Article 2(1) and the accompanying recital. The revised drafting focuses on whether the customer is granted ongoing access to services falling within the scope of the AML/CFT framework, and is intended to remain technologically neutral. AMLA agrees that subscriptions to newsletters, access to general information pages or other purely informational services should not, in themselves, be regarded as providing ongoing access to services falling within the scope of the AML/CFT framework. The final drafting therefore clarifies that the relevant consideration is ongoing access to AML/CFT-relevant services rather than the mere existence of a registration process.

3) Call for sector-specific guidance on the identification of business relationships and linked transactions Respondents expressed a need for additional sector-specific guidance, especially regarding Article 2(2) and Recital (8) of the draft RTS. More than thirty respondents, especially from the real estate, legal, gambling, accountancy, audit, art market and automotive sectors, considered that practical illustrative examples would significantly improve implementation. Stakeholders argued that generic criteria alone are insufficient to capture the diversity of business models covered by the AML framework. They argued that services connected to a single transaction may involve multiple interactions over an extended period without creating an ongoing business relationship. Some expressed concern that the concepts of repetition and duration could lead to the reclassification of isolated mandates as business relationships and requested sector-specific exemptions.
AMLA’s response:
AMLA acknowledges the concerns expressed by respondents regarding the application of the elements of duration and repetition, especially in certain non-financial sectors.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 19( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 29 These concepts may be more difficult to apply in sectors whose business models differ significantly from those of financial institutions, particularly where obliged entities provide services connected to transactions rather than carrying out transactions themselves. AMLA also recognises that supervisory approaches vary across Member States.

At the same time, RTS are a Level 2 instrument intended to establish legally binding provisions and are therefore not the appropriate instrument for including extensive practical examples or sector-specific case studies. Nor can it provide exemptions from Level 1. AMLA also notes that the concepts of business relationships and linked transactions are not new to the Union AML/CFT framework and were already present in previous AML Directives. The objective of the RTS is therefore to promote a more consistent interpretation across sectors and Member States. In light of the comments received, AMLA refined, via a new article (2(2)), the criteria related to the assessment of the elements of duration and repetition for obliged entities providing services connected to transactions. The provisions in Articles 2(2) and 2(3) are not cumulative. Where any one of the elements is present, this is sufficient to establish the existence of a business relationship.

To provide further clarity, AMLA intends to support implementation through non-binding explanatory material. A factsheet will be published when the final report is submitted to the European Commission, and AMLA is planning to publish additional explanatory material following the adoption of the RTS.

4) Sector specific criteria for identifying business relationships (money remitters, currency exchange, CASP) A substantial number of respondents commented on the operation of Article 2(3) and Recital 9, which use three transactions within a twelve-month period as an indicator of repetition for certain obliged entities from the financial sector. Respondents from payment institutions, remittance providers, crypto-asset service providers and other financial institutions considered that the criterion may be overly rigid and insufficiently sensitive to risk. Many argued that transaction frequency alone does not adequately capture the existence of an ongoing relationship and may generate unnecessary compliance burdens and false positives. Stakeholders frequently suggested complementing transaction counts with additional indicators such as transaction value, transaction purpose, customer risk profile or other qualitative factors. Several respondents also emphasised that the criterion should remain sector-specific and not be applied by analogy to obliged entities for which it was not designed.
AMLA’s response:

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 19( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 30 AMLA acknowledges respondents' concerns regarding the criterion set out in Article 2(4) (former Article 2(3)).

However, AMLA considers that the criterion remains justified. Supervisory experience demonstrates significant divergence across Member States in the identification of business relationships in the sectors concerned. Furthermore, these sectors consistently present elevated ML/TF risks according to the supra national risk assessment (SNRA).
The criterion therefore contributes to supervisory convergence and supports a more harmonised application of the concept of repetition throughout the Union.

AMLA highlights that the purpose of the RTS is not to redefine the AMLR concept of business relationship, as the definition is already in Level 1. Therefore, AMLA did not introduce additional value-based, behavioral or risk-based qualifiers, as these concepts are more relevant for the application of customer due diligence measures. No amendments were made to Article 2(4) as a result of these comments.

5) Sector specific criteria for identifying business relationships (gambling sector – physical premises) Respondents from the gambling sector raised concerns regarding the criterion contained in Article 2(4), which refers to engagement in gambling services through a membership arrangement.

Several stakeholders argued that membership alone should not be considered evidence of a business relationship, particularly where membership is required for technical or regulatory reasons. Respondents also suggested that other indicators, such as spending patterns or the continuity of activity, could be more relevant in assessing repetition. AMLA’s response:
AMLA acknowledges the concerns raised regarding the role of membership schemes in the assessment of repetition.

To address these comments, AMLA amended Article 2(5) (former Article 2(4)) to clarify that the relevant criterion concerns voluntary membership. Such membership may indicate an expectation of future engagement and may therefore be relevant when assessing the element of repetition.

AMLA did not introduce additional criteria based on transaction values, cumulative spending or behavioural indicators, as these elements are not part of the AMLR definition of business relationship and therefore fall outside the scope of these RTS.
F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 19( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 31

6) Sector specific criteria for identifying business relationships (Football sector) Respondents from the football sector commented on the criterion contained in Article 2(5), arguing that one-off player transfers should not automatically be considered indicators of a business relationship. Respondents also highlighted that significant safeguards already exist within the football sector and that many transfers do not involve continuing engagement between the parties.
AMLA’s response:
AMLA acknowledges the comments received from football clubs and sector representatives regarding one-off player transfers and FIFA-administered payments.

AMLA agrees that not all player transfers necessarily involve ongoing engagement between the parties. For this reason, the RTS focus on the existence of conditions attached to a transfer that may give rise to future actions or financial flows between the parties.

In response to the consultation feedback, AMLA amended Article 2(6) (former Article 2(5)) to further clarify the assessment of transfers involving conditional payment arrangements. The final drafting better reflects the distinction between isolated transfers and transfers giving rise to elements of duration or repetition.

7) Clarification of linked transaction criteria and prevention of false positives The scope of several criteria contained in Article 3(1) generated extensive feedback. Respondents questioned the practical application of indicators relating to family relationships, business partnerships, common intermediaries, loyalty programmes, digital infrastructure and customers operating in concert.

Respondents argued that these characteristics frequently arise in legitimate commercial or personal circumstances and do not necessarily indicate attempts to circumvent customer due diligence thresholds. Accordingly, many stakeholders advocated narrower definitions and requested that transactions be considered linked only where additional indications of coordination, common purpose or economic connection are present. Several respondents also called for greater clarity regarding commercially justified staged payments, instalment payments and sector-specific transaction patterns, arguing that such arrangements should not automatically be treated as linked transactions.

A significant number of respondents also raised operational concerns regarding the implementation of these criteria. They noted that some of the proposed indicators may be difficult to operationalise in automated systems and could result in a high number of false positives.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 19( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 32 Respondents from several sectors, namely the gambling, real-estate, and remittance sectors consider that transactions involving the same customer, common service providers or recurring commercial relationships are common business occurrences and do not necessarily indicate structuring or an attempt to circumvent CDD requirements.

Similar concerns were raised regarding the additional criterion applicable to gambling services under Article 3(3). Several respondents considered that certain gambling-specific transaction patterns or loyalty programmes may generate excessive numbers of false positives if not assessed in their proper commercial context.
AMLA’s response:

AMLA carefully considered the concerns raised regarding the potential generation of false positives and the practical application of the criteria set out in Article 3. AMLA acknowledges that certain indicators listed in Article 3 may also arise in legitimate commercial or personal circumstances. AMLA recalls that the definition of linked transactions is already in Level 1 and that the purpose of Article 3 is not to establish automatic linking rules, but to provide criteria that may assist obliged entities in assessing whether transactions meet the Level 1 definition. The existence of a particular criterion should therefore not, in itself, be regarded as sufficient to conclude that transactions are linked.

AMLA also notes that several comments appeared to reflect a degree of confusion between the identification of linked transactions for the purpose of applying occasional transaction thresholds and transaction scrutiny obligations applicable in the context of ongoing business relationships (Article 20 (f) AMLR).

In light of the comments received, AMLA amended Article 3 and the related recital to clarify more explicitly that the listed criteria form part of an overall assessment of the relevant facts and circumstances.

8) Information availability while identifying linked transactions and GDPR Comments relating to Article 3(1)(b) and Recital 11 highlighted significant concerns regarding the practical availability of information and the interaction of the RTS with data protection requirements. Several respondents from legal, notarial, accountancy, audit, real-estate and artmarket sectors argued that they frequently lack access to information relating to family relationships, business partnerships, beneficial ownership structures or digital identifiers. Many requested clarification that the criteria should be applied solely on the basis of information already available in the ordinary course of business and that obliged entities should not be expected to collect additional information solely for the purposes of the RTS. Several respondents

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 19( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 33 also highlighted potential conflicts with GDPR principles and requested explicit safeguards within the RTS.
AMLA’s response AMLA welcomes the detailed feedback concerning information availability and data-protection considerations.

AMLA agrees that obliged entities should not be required to obtain additional information solely for the purpose of identifying linked transactions. Equally, AMLA considers that the identification of linked transactions remains compatible with the Union data-protection framework and should be based on information that is already available to the obliged entities. To provide greater certainty, AMLA refined the recital accompanying Article 3 to clarify the meaning of information available to the obliged entity and to confirm that the RTS do not create an obligation to collect additional information solely for the purpose of identifying linked transactions.

9) Clarification of temporal concepts and aggregation periods for linked transactions A large number of comments focused on the temporal elements contained in Article 3(1)(e) and Recital 17. Respondents emphasised that transaction cycles differ significantly between sectors and argued that the notions of a "short period of time", or "specific period" require greater clarification. Financial institutions seek benchmarks to avoid supervisory divergence. Real estate and legal sector argue for longer period due to transactions cycles. Gambling and remitters prefer short windows to reflect high frequency activity. Some respondents called to have sector specific timeframe (for instance 1 day for gambling, 12 months for real estate).

Regarding the one-month period set out for some targeted sectors in Article 3(2), the respondents noted that this fixed timeframe may produce either over-identification or under-identification of linked transactions. Instead, they advocated a more flexible approach supported by sectorspecific examples that better reflect the nature and risk profile of different business models. AMLA’s response AMLA acknowledges the comments received regarding the temporal elements used for identifying linked transactions and the requests for greater specificity regarding the concept of “short timeframe".

AMLA considers that transaction cycles, transaction frequencies and ML/TF risks differ significantly not only between sectors, but could also differ between obliged entities operating within the same sector. As a result, AMLA does not consider that introducing a single harmonised

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 19( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 34 timeframe, or predefined timeframes for individual sectors, would be consistent with the riskbased approach underpinning Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

AMLA therefore considers that obliged entities are best placed to assess what constitutes a "short timeframe" in light of the nature of their business, the speed and frequency with which transactions are typically carried out, and their size. This assessment should form part of the obliged entity's overall assessment of the relevant facts and circumstances. For these reasons, AMLA retained the risk-based approach reflected in Article 3(1)(e) and confirmed that the prescriptive approach retained in Article 3(2) remains justified for the limited number of sectors covered by that provision and therefore made no changes to that article.

10) Broad support for maintaining the current framework on thresholds for occasional transactions Feedback on the provisions implementing Article 19(9) AMLR demonstrated broad support for the approach reflected in Recital 18. Approximately 120 respondents, representing both financial and non-financial sectors, agreed that there is currently insufficient evidence to justify introducing additional lower thresholds for occasional transactions. Respondents generally argued that existing AMLR thresholds already reflect sector-specific risks and that additional reductions would increase compliance costs and customer friction without delivering proportionate AML/CFT benefits. Although a small minority of respondents advocated targeted thresholds for specific sectors such as precious metals, cultural goods or certain payment services, these proposals did not attract broad support. Many respondents nevertheless encouraged AMLA to review the issue periodically on the basis of supervisory experience, risk assessments and empirical evidence.
AMLA’s response:
AMLA welcomes the broad support expressed for the proposed approach regarding additional lower thresholds.
Consequently, AMLA maintained the approach proposed in the consultation paper and did not introduce additional lower thresholds in the final RTS.
AMLA will nevertheless continue to monitor supervisory experience and developments in ML/TF risks and may reassess this issue in the future should new evidence emerge.
